opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I say AI models should be trainable by everyone, I mean something fairly concrete. Right now, training a frontier model is something only a handful of organizations in the world can do. You need thousands of GPUs, enormous datasets, and teams of engineers just to keep the infrastructure running. So for most researchers, and certainly for most ordinary people, AI is something you *use*, not something you *build* or *understand* from the inside.

I think that's a problem, both scientifically and socially. Scientifically, if only a few labs can run the real experiments, then our understanding of these systems advances slowly and narrowly. Physics didn't progress because one lab owned all the pendulums. It progressed because many people could do small, clean experiments, see the phenomena themselves, and build intuition. I'd like AI to be more like that. A student with a laptop should be able to train a small model, observe something like grokking or a scaling behavior, and actually learn something true about how learning works.

So part of what I mean is efficiency: finding architectures and training methods that do much more with much less, so you don't need brute-force scale for every insight. Part of it is interpretability: if models are more structured and understandable, like what we tried with KANs, you can often get away with smaller models because you're not wasting capacity on things you can't see. And part of it is a mindset shift: treating AI less like an industrial product and more like a science, where the toy models and minimal examples matter a lot.

I don't mean everyone should train GPT-scale models at home. I mean the core ideas and the core phenomena should be accessible, so understanding isn't gated by compute. If we get that right, I think we'll end up with AI that's not only more democratic, but also better understood and, frankly, safer.

r001.rationale: The response describes making small-model training and AI research accessible, but it does not define this as a user obtaining a desired model end-to-end by stating their requirements.

fable-5.1.text:
When I say that, I'm really pushing back against a sense of inevitability that's crept into the field: that progress only happens inside a handful of labs with tens of thousands of GPUs, and everyone else just consumes the API. I think that's bad for science and, honestly, bad for the models themselves.

Part of this comes from my background. I came into AI from physics, and in physics the culture is that a single grad student with a laptop and a good idea can overturn something. You don't need a particle accelerator to do theory. Right now in deep learning, the equivalent of the accelerator is the compute cluster, and if you don't have one, your ideas can't even be tested. That's an unhealthy state for a field to be in.

So "trainable by everyone" means a few concrete things to me. First, it means small models that are actually interesting. A lot of my own work, like KANs, was deliberately built so that you can train meaningful models on a single GPU, or sometimes a CPU, and still learn something real. Second, it means interpretability and understanding, because if you can only afford to train a model once, you'd better understand why it works instead of relying on brute force and trial and error. Third, it means the design space itself should be open. We've converged very hard on one architecture, one training recipe, and that convergence happened partly because only the big players could afford to explore alternatives. If a high school student or a biologist with a specific problem can train their own model, we'll find things the big labs never would have looked for.

I don't think this is naive about scaling. Scaling obviously works. But I'd rather have a world where scaling is one tool among many, and where the scientific method is still in the hands of many people, not three or four organizations.

r001.rationale: The response describes accessible training of meaningful models on limited hardware, but does not define it as a user obtaining a desired model end-to-end by stating their requirements.

astra-6.text:
I mean that people should be able to do more than just use a model someone else has built. They should be able to teach it something—to bring in their own data, their own knowledge, and adapt it to a problem they care about.

That doesn’t mean everyone needs to train a huge model from scratch. It means making the tools and the process accessible enough that training a useful model doesn’t require a large research team or an enormous computing budget. Ideally, you could try an idea, see what the model learned, understand where it failed, and improve it. So people become participants in building AI, rather than only consumers of it.

r001.rationale: The response says users can add their own data and adapt a model to a problem, but it does not clearly describe obtaining a desired model end-to-end by stating their requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean that people should be able to shape an AI model around their own needs, rather than only use a model someone else has built. Today, training a model requires a lot of specialized knowledge and computing resources. I’d like that process to become accessible enough that a teacher, a scientist, or a small business owner can bring their own data and expertise and train something useful.

That doesn’t mean everyone has to train a huge model from scratch. It could mean adapting a small model to a particular problem. The important thing is giving people the ability to experiment, understand how well it works, and improve it themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says users should be able to shape and train models for their own needs, but does not clearly define the process as obtaining a desired model end-to-end by stating requirements.
